VIDEO.title: What Jesus REALLY Wants You to ASK Him! (Matthew 7:1-12)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: The ask passage explains the judging passage.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 7:1-12: do not judge, the speck and the log, pearls before swine, ask, seek and knock, the father who gives good gifts, and the golden rule.
Jesus turns to judging inside the community of disciples (7:1-5), warns against engaging certain people (7:6), teaches about asking God (7:7-11), and sums it all up with the golden rule (7:12).

Nothing here is a new subject. 7:1-12 continues the unit that began at 6:19, and words like 'hypocrite' and 'the Law and the Prophets' send the listener back to earlier parts of the sermon. These practical teachings are applications of the Beatitudes.
Hypocritical, condemning judgment is the same bad eye as greed (6:19-24) and worry (6:25-34). The speck and the log trade on 'the eye is the lamp of the body' (6:22-23).

Ask, seek, knock is the other side of the coin from worry: chapter 6 shows a passive trust in the Father, chapter 7 an active one. The ask passage (7:7-11) explains the judging passage (7:1-6): judging another's worth comes from not trusting the Father.

The apostles repeat the lesson: Romans 14:4, 1 Corinthians 4:5, James 2:12-13 and Galatians 6:1-2. For a disciple, judging looks like restoration and bearing a brother's burden, and it starts with trusting the Father.
QUOTES: All of these things build from the previous thing that Jesus just said; all of it is connected.
If you are condemnatory and a hypocrite, it means you have a bad eye.
The ask passage is the explanation for the judgment passage.
The judgment that disciples of Jesus are called to make demands having a good eye, which trades on completely trusting the Father first.
Trust that the Father will do what is right in all situations and for all people.

LSB_QUOTES.text: You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.
Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
Therefore, in all things, whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

JUDGE.kicker: The speck and the log · Matthew 7:1-5
JUDGE.title: First take the log out

src.text: And why do you look at the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ and behold, the log is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.

lines.text: Jesus is not banning every judgment: first take the log out, then help your brother. The picture is an eye on purpose. Condemning, hypocritical judgment is the bad eye of 6:22-23, the same eye that is greedy and anxious.
'You hypocrite' should send the disciples back to the hypocrites of 6:2, 5 and 16, who give, pray and fast to be seen.
Rabbinic teaching knew the same picture: if one says 'Remove the splinter from between your eyes,' the other answers, 'Remove the beam from between your eyes' (Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 16b).
'Judge' is krinō (G2919): to decide, judge in court, or condemn. 'With what measure you measure' (7:2) is the language of the market; Luke adds 'pardon, and you will be pardoned' (Luke 6:37).

src.text: Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.

left.text: Do not reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you, / Reprove a wise man and he will love you.

right.text: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, / For he will despise the insight of your speech.

lines.text: Verse 6 is a qualifier for correcting others. Once you have learned to correct humbly, remember that not everyone should be corrected: Proverbs warns against engaging scoffers, mockers and fools.

Dogs and pigs were unclean animals to Jews (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8). Readers have taken 'what is holy' and 'pearls' as the gospel, holy things, or wise rebuke; Chrysostom applies it to people fixed in ungodliness.

JUDGE.title: This is the Law and the Prophets

src.text: Therefore, in all things, whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

lines.text: Jesus sums up the whole teaching with the golden rule. 'The Law and the Prophets' takes the listener back to 5:17, where the main body of the sermon began.

A famous saying of Hillel, from a generation before Jesus, puts it negatively: 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation' (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Jesus states it positively. Compare 'love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39-40).

left.text: do not be worried about your life, as to what you will eat or what you will drink; nor for your body, as to what you will put on.

right.text: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

lines.text: The new teaching on asking is the other side of the coin from worry and anxiety.

left.text: Look at the birds of the air, that they do not sow, nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?

right.text: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give what is good to those who ask Him!

lines.text: God provides for the birds and the flowers; if earthly fathers give good gifts, how much more will God.
Luke's version ends, 'how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him?' (Luke 11:13).

left.text: But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

right.text: For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened.

lines.text: The same verb, zēteō (G2212), is in both verses.

COIN.title: Keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking

left.text: for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.

right.text: how much more will your Father who is in heaven give what is good to those who ask Him!

lines.text: Chapter 6 shows a passive trust in God; chapter 7 an active one: ask, seek, knock, and keep doing it.

The three verbs in 7:7 are present imperatives in Greek, which can carry the sense 'keep on asking.' Chrysostom: 'to this end He said, knock, to signify that even if He should not straightway open the door, we are to continue there' (Homilies on Matthew 23).

src.text: Who are you to judge the servant of another? To his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

lines.text: What is required to accept this verse? Trust.

src.text: Therefore do not go on passing judgment before the time, but wait until the Lord comes who will both bring to light the things hidden in the darkness and make manifest the motives of hearts.

lines.text: Again, accepting this takes trust that the Lord will judge rightly.

src.text: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of freedom. For judgment will be merciless to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

lines.text: James repeats Jesus' teaching, and the Beatitude: 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy' (5:7).

src.text: Brothers, even if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, each of you looking to yourself, so that you too will not be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

lines.text: What does judging look like for a disciple of Jesus? Restoration, and bearing your brother's burden.
'Restore' (katartizō) is used of mending nets (Matthew 4:21). 'Looking to yourself' is the log check of 7:5.

TERMS.def: To decide, to judge in court, or to condemn. Jesus forbids condemning, hypocritical judgment, not all discernment (7:5-6).
Originally a stage actor. In the sermon: people who perform righteousness to be seen (6:2, 5, 16) and who see the speck but not the log (7:5).
A unit of thought in Scripture. The video treats 6:19-7:12 as one unit.
A mirrored pattern. The video reads the whole sermon as a chiasm, so later sayings echo earlier ones.
In Proverbs, a mocker who refuses correction (9:7-8; 15:12).
7:12, 'whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them.' The name is later, not biblical.
Shorthand for the Scriptures of Israel (5:17; 7:12; 22:40).
The Hebrew idiom from 6:22: a generous, loving way of seeing people. The video's theme for 6:19-7:12.

WORDS.gloss: To judge, decide; in context, to condemn. Look up: BDAG, κρίνω.
Speck, splinter, a bit of straw or wood.
Dog; a scavenger, not a pet.
Scoffer, mocker: one who will not take correction.

BACKGROUND.p: A carpenter's joke: a tiny splinter against a roof beam. The Talmud records the same pair as a proverb about people who will not accept rebuke (Arakhin 16b).
Dogs were mostly street scavengers, and pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7). Both pictures describe people who do not value what is offered and may turn on the giver.

BACKGROUND.h: Bread and stones, fish and snakes
BACKGROUND.p: Flat round loaves could look like stones, and some fish of the lake look like snakes. A good father would never trick a hungry child, and neither will God.

The Mishnah keeps Hillel's saying 'Do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place' (Avot 2:4) and Joshua ben Perahiah's 'judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor' (Avot 1:6). The video's point: many rabbis taught not to take God's place in judging a person's worth.

WITNESSES.text: Do you see, that He forbids not judging, but commands to cast out first the beam from your eye, and then to set right the doings of the rest of the world?
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 23, on 7:1-5. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: For to this end was the door shut, that He may induce you to knock: to this end He does not straightway assent, that you may ask.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 23, on 7:7. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: So that if perchance, for example, he has transgressed in anger, you should find fault in hatred; there being, as it were, as much difference between anger and hatred as between a mote and a beam.
WITNESSES.src: On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 6 (public domain).

DEBATES.h: Does 'do not judge' forbid all judging?
DEBATES.p: Almost all readers say no: 7:5 expects the log-free disciple to help, 7:6 and 7:15-20 require discernment, and Matthew 18:15-17 sets out how to correct a brother. What is forbidden is hypocritical, condemning judgment.

DEBATES.h: What do the dogs and pigs mean?
DEBATES.p: Suggestions: people who scorn correction (the video, with Proverbs); people hostile to the gospel; or a warning to protect holy things. The early church used 7:6 to keep the Lord's Supper for the baptized (Didache 9).
Some see a new topic (prayer). The video reads asking as the answer to judging: trust the Father to do right, and you will not condemn. Others link 7:7-11 back to the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13).
Many outlines treat 6:19-7:12 as the last block before the conclusion, framed by 'the Law and the Prophets' (5:17; 7:12). The chiastic outline of the whole sermon is a proposal.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Jesus says 'not if you judge, when you judge.' The text says 'Do not judge' (7:1). The point still holds from 7:5, which expects the disciple to help a brother once the log is out.
In the side-by-side chart, 'Your Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask' is 7:11 (the captions say 7:1). 'Verses 1:1' means 7:1.

The saying 'your blood is no redder' comes from the Talmud (Pesachim 25b; Sanhedrin 74a), where it is about refusing to kill someone to save your own life, not about judging. The closer saying is Hillel's 'Do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place' (Mishnah Avot 2:4).
The video gives no source for its three definitions of judgment in Jesus' day. The Greek krinō does cover all three senses (a court verdict, deciding, condemning), so the categories fit the word.
James 2:12 reads 'the law of freedom' in the LSB, and Romans 14:4 reads 'Who are you to judge the servant of another?'

QUESTIONS: Whose 'speck' have you been noticing lately? What might the 'log' in your own eye be?
The video links condemning others to worry and greed: all the bad eye. Where do you see that connection in your own life?
When is it wise not to correct someone (7:6)? How do you tell a scoffer from someone who wants help?
Ask, seek, knock: what have you stopped asking God for? What would keeping on look like?
Galatians 6:1 says to restore 'in a spirit of gentleness.' Think of a time someone restored you gently. What did they do?
The video asks how this lesson applies to you in your situation. Write one sentence.
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: the judgment disciples of Jesus are called to make demands having a good eye, and that trades on completely trusting the Father first. A disciple who trusts the Father becomes self-reflective when he sees a speck in his brother's eye, handles it with reverence, forgives first, and helps out of radical generosity. Ask, seek, knock means trusting that the Father will do what is right in all situations and for all people. Now think about how it applies directly to your life.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before correcting anyone this week, do the log check of Galatians 6:1: pray first, name one fault of your own, and decide whether the person is ready to hear (Proverbs 9:8). If you go, go to restore, not to win.

# Matthew 7:1-12 Study Notes: What Jesus REALLY Wants You to ASK Him! (Matthew 7:1-12)
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4STV81KbSsw
Channel: Every Word | Length: 21:20 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 7:1-12: do not judge, the speck and the log, pearls before swine, ask, seek and knock, the father who gives good gifts, and the golden rule.
- Jesus turns to judging inside the community of disciples (7:1-5), warns against engaging certain people (7:6), teaches about asking God (7:7-11), and sums it all up with the golden rule (7:12).
- Nothing here is a new subject. 7:1-12 continues the unit that began at 6:19, and words like 'hypocrite' and 'the Law and the Prophets' send the listener back to earlier parts of the sermon. These practical teachings are applications of the Beatitudes.
- Hypocritical, condemning judgment is the same bad eye as greed (6:19-24) and worry (6:25-34). The speck and the log trade on 'the eye is the lamp of the body' (6:22-23).
- Ask, seek, knock is the other side of the coin from worry: chapter 6 shows a passive trust in the Father, chapter 7 an active one. The ask passage (7:7-11) explains the judging passage (7:1-6): judging another's worth comes from not trusting the Father.
- The apostles repeat the lesson: Romans 14:4, 1 Corinthians 4:5, James 2:12-13 and Galatians 6:1-2. For a disciple, judging looks like restoration and bearing a brother's burden, and it starts with trusting the Father.

> "All of these things build from the previous thing that Jesus just said; all of it is connected."
> "If you are condemnatory and a hypocrite, it means you have a bad eye."

### Lay the pages side by side
The teacher's tip: open your Bible flat and read 7:1-12 with chapter 6 beside it. Each time you meet a word you have heard before ('hypocrite,' 'eye,' 'seek,' 'Father,' 'the Law and the Prophets'), ask how the earlier mention helps you understand this one.

## Worry or ask: two sides of one coin
Chapter 6 and chapter 7, side by side
A Matthew 6:25 do not be worried about your life
    B Matthew 6:26 your heavenly Father feeds them
        C Matthew 6:33 But seek first His kingdom
        C' Matthew 7:7 Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find
    B' Matthew 7:11 how much more will your Father who is in heaven give what is good to those who ask Him!
Passive trust (chapter 6) becomes active trust (chapter 7).
1. Worry or ask · 6:25 and 7:7: Do not worry; ask
   Chapter 6 (Matthew 6:25, LSB): "do not be worried about your life, as to what you will eat or what you will drink; nor for your body, as to what you will put on."
   Chapter 7 (Matthew 7:7, LSB): "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."
   (video) The new teaching on asking is the other side of the coin from worry and anxiety.
2. The Father provides · 6:26 and 7:11: How much more
   Chapter 6 (Matthew 6:26, LSB): "Look at the birds of the air, that they do not sow, nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?"
   Chapter 7 (Matthew 7:11, LSB): "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give what is good to those who ask Him!"
   (video) God provides for the birds and the flowers; if earthly fathers give good gifts, how much more will God.
   [Background] Luke's version ends, 'how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him?' (Luke 11:13). (Luke 11:9-13)
3. Seek · 6:33 and 7:7: Seek first; seek and find
   Chapter 6 (Matthew 6:33, LSB): "But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you."
   Chapter 7 (Matthew 7:8, LSB): "For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened."
   [Background] The same verb, zēteō (G2212), is in both verses.
4. Passive and active trust: Keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking
   Chapter 6 (Matthew 6:32, LSB): "for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things."
   Chapter 7 (Matthew 7:11, LSB): "how much more will your Father who is in heaven give what is good to those who ask Him!"
   (video) Chapter 6 shows a passive trust in God; chapter 7 an active one: ask, seek, knock, and keep doing it.
   [Background] The three verbs in 7:7 are present imperatives in Greek, which can carry the sense 'keep on asking.' Chrysostom: 'to this end He said, knock, to signify that even if He should not straightway open the door, we are to continue there' (Homilies on Matthew 23).

## Key people
- Jesus: Teaches His disciples how to judge as disciples: humbly, mercifully, trusting the Father. [Background] Later He shows what restoring looks like: He restores Peter after his denial (John 21:15-19).
- The disciples: Still sitting at His feet; they should connect each saying to what He has already taught. [Background] Later Jesus gives them a pattern for correcting a brother: first privately (Matthew 18:15-17).
- The hypocrite: Sees the speck, not the log: the bad eye in action. [Background] The same word as the showy givers, prayers and fasters of 6:2, 5, 16.
- Scoffers and fools: Proverbs' warning behind 7:6: not everyone will receive correction. [Background] 'He who disciplines a scoffer receives disgrace for himself' (Proverbs 9:7).
- Hillel: The video quotes 'an ancient Jewish saying' about judging; the saying is credited to Hillel. [Background] A leading teacher a generation before Jesus. 'Do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place' (Mishnah Avot 2:4).

## Places [Background]
- Mount of Beatitudes: The traditional site of the sermon.
- Capernaum: Jesus' home base (4:13), with fishing boats and nets.
- Tabgha: A spring-fed cove near the traditional mount.
- Magdala: A busy fishing town: fish, the everyday food of 7:10.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital, with its own court system.
- Bethsaida: Home town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Hippos: A Gentile city across the lake, where pigs were raised (compare 7:6 and 8:30).

## Key terms
- Judge (krinō): To decide, to judge in court, or to condemn. Jesus forbids condemning, hypocritical judgment, not all discernment (7:5-6). [Background]
- Hypocrite: Originally a stage actor. In the sermon: people who perform righteousness to be seen (6:2, 5, 16) and who see the speck but not the log (7:5).
- Pericope: A unit of thought in Scripture. The video treats 6:19-7:12 as one unit.
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern. The video reads the whole sermon as a chiasm, so later sayings echo earlier ones.
- Scoffer (lets): In Proverbs, a mocker who refuses correction (9:7-8; 15:12).
- Golden rule: 7:12, 'whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them.' The name is later, not biblical. [Background]
- The Law and the Prophets: Shorthand for the Scriptures of Israel (5:17; 7:12; 22:40).
- Good eye: The Hebrew idiom from 6:22: a generous, loving way of seeing people. The video's theme for 6:19-7:12.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Specks and logs: A carpenter's joke: a tiny splinter against a roof beam. The Talmud records the same pair as a proverb about people who will not accept rebuke (Arakhin 16b).
- Dogs and pigs: Dogs were mostly street scavengers, and pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7). Both pictures describe people who do not value what is offered and may turn on the giver.
- Bread and stones, fish and snakes: Flat round loaves could look like stones, and some fish of the lake look like snakes. A good father would never trick a hungry child, and neither will God.
- Judging in the Jewish tradition: The Mishnah keeps Hillel's saying 'Do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place' (Avot 2:4) and Joshua ben Perahiah's 'judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor' (Avot 1:6). The video's point: many rabbis taught not to take God's place in judging a person's worth.

- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For to this end was the door shut, that He may induce you to knock: to this end He does not straightway assent, that you may ask." Homilies on Matthew 23, on 7:7. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- Augustine of Hippo (c. AD 393): "So that if perchance, for example, he has transgressed in anger, you should find fault in hatred; there being, as it were, as much difference between anger and hatred as between a mote and a beam." On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 6 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Does 'do not judge' forbid all judging? Almost all readers say no: 7:5 expects the log-free disciple to help, 7:6 and 7:15-20 require discernment, and Matthew 18:15-17 sets out how to correct a brother. What is forbidden is hypocritical, condemning judgment.
- What do the dogs and pigs mean? Suggestions: people who scorn correction (the video, with Proverbs); people hostile to the gospel; or a warning to protect holy things. The early church used 7:6 to keep the Lord's Supper for the baptized (Didache 9).
- How does 7:7-11 connect to 7:1-6? Some see a new topic (prayer). The video reads asking as the answer to judging: trust the Father to do right, and you will not condemn. Others link 7:7-11 back to the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13).
- Is 6:19-7:12 one unit? Many outlines treat 6:19-7:12 as the last block before the conclusion, framed by 'the Law and the Prophets' (5:17; 7:12). The chiastic outline of the whole sermon is a proposal.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Jesus says 'not if you judge, when you judge.' The text says 'Do not judge' (7:1). The point still holds from 7:5, which expects the disciple to help a brother once the log is out.
- In the side-by-side chart, 'Your Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask' is 7:11 (the captions say 7:1). 'Verses 1:1' means 7:1.
- The saying 'your blood is no redder' comes from the Talmud (Pesachim 25b; Sanhedrin 74a), where it is about refusing to kill someone to save your own life, not about judging. The closer saying is Hillel's 'Do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place' (Mishnah Avot 2:4).
- The video gives no source for its three definitions of judgment in Jesus' day. The Greek krinō does cover all three senses (a court verdict, deciding, condemning), so the categories fit the word.
- James 2:12 reads 'the law of freedom' in the LSB, and Romans 14:4 reads 'Who are you to judge the servant of another?'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Whose 'speck' have you been noticing lately? What might the 'log' in your own eye be?
2. The video links condemning others to worry and greed: all the bad eye. Where do you see that connection in your own life?
3. When is it wise not to correct someone (7:6)? How do you tell a scoffer from someone who wants help?
4. Ask, seek, knock: what have you stopped asking God for? What would keeping on look like?
5. Galatians 6:1 says to restore 'in a spirit of gentleness.' Think of a time someone restored you gently. What did they do?
6. The video asks how this lesson applies to you in your situation. Write one sentence.

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: the judgment disciples of Jesus are called to make demands having a good eye, and that trades on completely trusting the Father first. A disciple who trusts the Father becomes self-reflective when he sees a speck in his brother's eye, handles it with reverence, forgives first, and helps out of radical generosity. Ask, seek, knock means trusting that the Father will do what is right in all situations and for all people. Now think about how it applies directly to your life.
- Study note (added): before correcting anyone this week, do the log check of Galatians 6:1: pray first, name one fault of your own, and decide whether the person is ready to hear (Proverbs 9:8). If you go, go to restore, not to win.
